prompt.context: Our client provides satellite TV service nationwide. Its customer base is being threatened by telcos and cable companies offering 'triple play' bundles of TV, internet, and phone services. The client is considering deploying a WiMAX wireless network across the USA to offer its customers broadband internet (and potentially phone service via VoIP), which would allow it to compete with triple-play offerings.
prompt.question: Should our client go into the broadband (WiMAX) business?

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of the broadband internet market and what market share does management estimate?
clarifying_info.a: Management estimates the client could achieve 5% market share of US broadband subscribers.

clarifying_info.q: What is the pricing for broadband internet service?
clarifying_info.a: Broadband internet service would be priced at $20 per month.

clarifying_info.q: What are the technical parameters for the WiMAX network?
clarifying_info.a: Each base station has 80,000 kbps of bandwidth; each household requires 320 kbps; assume 50% of subscribers are online concurrently at any point in time.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost of customer premise equipment (CPE)?
clarifying_info.a: CPE costs $150 per household; the client estimates 2/3 of that cost could be passed through to the customer.

clarifying_info.q: Should we consider building or leasing base stations?
clarifying_info.a: Both options exist. Build (own and operate) costs ~$380K per base station in CAPEX and OPEX; leasing costs ~$150K per base station in OPEX.

exhibits.title: Spectrum Auction Prices
exhibits.shows: A bar chart of historical spectrum auction prices paid by major telecom companies (Verizon, T-Mobile, Comcast, AT&T) from May 2005 to Sep 2007, with an average line.

exhibits.title: Base Station Count Calculation
exhibits.shows: A diagram showing the derivation of the number of base stations required, using US population, persons per household, market share, base station bandwidth, household bandwidth, and concurrent connection rate.

exhibits.title: Incremental Revenue vs. Costs Summary
exhibits.shows: A summary table comparing total investment costs (spectrum, base stations, CPE, SG&A) against potential revenue from broadband internet subscribers.

framework: Quantify total investment costs: spectrum license, base station build/lease, customer premise equipment (CPE), SG&A
Estimate potential revenues: addressable market size, realistic market share, pricing
Calculate whether the investment breaks even and over what timeframe
Assess strategic and qualitative risks: competitive response, regulatory hurdles, buy-vs-build tradeoffs, timing
Synthesize: does the financial return justify the investment, and what are alternatives for defending the core satellite TV business?

questions.prompt: What is the cost of acquiring spectrum, and what assumption should we use?
questions.guidance: Candidate should look at the historical spectrum auction data (Exhibit 1), note the range of prices paid ($240M–$1,100M), identify the average, and use ~$500M as the assumed spectrum cost.

math.setup: Use the average of historical spectrum auction prices as a proxy.
steps: Observe auction prices ranging from $240M (Mar-2007 Verizon) to $1,100M (May-2005 Verizon)
Visual average from chart is approximately $500M

questions.prompt: How many base stations are required to cover the serviceable customer base?
questions.guidance: Candidate must derive households from US population, apply market share, then use bandwidth parameters to calculate households per base station and total base stations needed.

math.setup: Number of base stations = Serviceable households / Households per base station; Households per base station = Base station bandwidth / (Bandwidth per household x Concurrent connection rate)
steps: US households = 300M population / 2.5 persons per household = 120M households
Serviceable households (target market) = 120M (all US households are addressable; market share applied to subscribers, not to coverage)
Households per base station = 80,000 kbps / (320 kbps x 50%) = 80,000 / 160 = 500 households per base station
Number of base stations = 120M / 500 = 240,000 — NOTE: the casebook simplifies by applying 5% market share to base station count: 120M x 5% = 6M target subscribers; 6M / 500 = 12,000 base stations

questions.prompt: What is the total cost of base stations, and should the client build or lease?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compare build vs. lease on both quantitative (cost) and qualitative (time-to-market, control) dimensions, then recommend lease as the lower-investment option. Total base station cost = 12,000 x $150K = $1.8B.

math.setup: Base station cost = Number of base stations x Cost per base station
steps: Build option: ~$380K per base station (CAPEX + OPEX for planning, electronics, cabling, maintenance)
Lease option: ~$150K per base station (OPEX: tower lease, backhaul lease, electronics, cabling, maintenance)
Recommendation: lease to minimize upfront investment and accelerate time-to-market
Total base station cost (lease): 12,000 x $150K = $1,800M

questions.prompt: What is the net cost of customer premise equipment (CPE)?
questions.guidance: CPE is $150 per household for 6M subscribers; 2/3 can be passed through to the customer, so the client bears 1/3.

math.setup: CPE net cost = Total CPE cost x (1 - pass-through rate)
steps: Total CPE cost = 6M households x $150 = $900M
Client pass-through = 2/3 of cost to customer, so client bears 1/3
CPE net cost to client = $900M x (1/3) = $300M

questions.prompt: What is the total investment and what is the annual revenue potential? Does this make financial sense in year 1?
questions.guidance: Candidate should sum all costs and compare to first-year revenue. Total cost = $2.6B; first-year revenue = $1.44B. The investment cannot break even in year 1 — costs exceed revenue by over $1B.

math.setup: Total cost = Spectrum + Base stations + CPE + SG&A; Revenue = Subscribers x Monthly price x 12 months
steps: Spectrum: $500M
Base stations (lease): $1,800M
CPE (net): $300M
SG&A: assumed minimal initially
Total cost: ~$2,600M ($2.6B)
Revenue: 6M subscribers x $20/mo x 12 months = $1,440M ($1.44B)
Gap: $2,600M - $1,440M = $1,160M shortfall in year 1
math.answer: Total investment $2.6B vs. revenue $1.44B; cannot break even in year 1

brainstorming.prompt: If the client should not pursue WiMAX, what strategic alternatives should it consider to defend its core satellite TV business?

categories.name: Customer segmentation and profitability
ideas: Segment customers and increase share with the most profitable segments
Focus retention spending on high-value subscribers

categories.name: Scale and cost efficiency
ideas: Grow subscriber scale to reduce cost per subscriber
Negotiate better content and infrastructure deals as scale increases

categories.name: Content differentiation
ideas: Pursue acquisition or partnership to drive differentiated content
Invest in exclusive or premium programming unavailable on competing platforms

categories.name: Technology and product innovation
ideas: Offer DVR capabilities to compete with cable's video-on-demand
Increase number of local and national HD channels

categories.name: Partnership for broadband
ideas: Partner with telcos to offer broadband where telcos are not building video infrastructure
Pursue wholesale or white-label broadband arrangements rather than building own network

recommendation: Investment in a WiMAX network probably does not make sense: total upfront cost of ~$2.6B exceeds first-year revenue of ~$1.44B, with no clear path to break-even in year 1
The client should focus on defending and strengthening its core satellite TV business rather than entering the capital-intensive broadband market
risks: Market pricing for broadband may compress further, reducing revenue assumptions
Timing risk: WiMAX deployment could take years, during which customer attrition from triple-play competitors continues
Technology risk: WiMAX may be displaced by alternative technologies (e.g., LTE)
Additional costs (SG&A, ongoing operations) could widen the investment gap
Competitive response from telcos and cable could further erode satellite TV market share even if client launches WiMAX
next_steps: Segment the satellite TV customer base and prioritize retention of high-value subscribers
Evaluate content acquisition or partnership opportunities to differentiate the satellite TV offering
Explore DVR rollout and expansion of HD channels to compete with cable's VOD
Assess partnership opportunities with telcos for broadband access on a wholesale basis
Monitor WiMAX technology economics and revisit the business case if spectrum/equipment costs fall materially
